A1.justification: Both readable PDFs describe the same incremental weather-forecasting work, renamed from CA-MoE to VA-MoE. Their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. Neither contains an appendix; supplementary material referenced in v1 is not included and cannot supply evidence.

before.justification: V1 reports original ERA5 forecasting experiments, architecture comparisons, incremental-learning results and expert-channel visualizations in Tables 2–3 and Figures 4–6.

after.justification: V2 reports original ERA5 forecasting results, full versus incremental training comparisons, reduced-data experiments and architecture comparisons in Tables 2–4 and Figures 1 and 4–5.

M1.justification: The renamed method retains index-guided channel Top-K routing, variable-specific and shared experts, frozen existing experts during expansion, encoder/decoder extension, dynamic prediction weighting and reconstruction loss. Additional equations and index-encoder explanations document existing components rather than establish a different algorithm.

E1.justification: Both use ERA5 with the same upper-air variables, pressure levels and five possible surface variables. V1 evaluates both three-variable and five-variable surface expansion; v2 retains only the five-variable scenario. MSL and SP already participate in v1, so their newly displayed scores do not establish new variable coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds GraphCast and Stormer to Figure 4, and adds ClimaX, GraphCast, FengWu and FuXi to the surface-variable comparison in Table 2. GraphCast also enters the upper-air comparison. The ViT and ViT+MoE architecture comparators remain, moving from v1 Table 3 to v2 Table 4.

E3.justification: V1 evaluates its model primarily at 128×256 against higher-resolution competitors; v2 reports common 721×1440 resolution for the main comparisons, retaining 128×256 architecture experiments. V2 introduces 2000–2020 incremental training alongside 1979–2020 training and reports 400,000, 200,000 and 100,000 iteration settings. The reported incremental parameter count changes from approximately 107M to 137M.

E4.justification: Supporting analyses shift toward training efficiency: v2 adds full-training controls and comparisons across incremental data/iteration budgets in Table 2 and Figure 1. It removes v1's three-versus-five-variable sensitivity comparison and Figure 6's expert-channel selection analysis. The architecture comparison is retained and reorganized as Table 4, while Figure 5's forecast visualization is retained.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates or statistical significance tests for its experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 and Figure 4 contain extensive numerical revisions and new results, including MSL/SP scores and training-budget comparisons. At the retained 128×256 grid, initial-model 72-hour Z500 RMSE changes from 152.7 to 139.02. Pangu-Weather's full-resolution 72-hour Z500 entry changes from 139.8 to 167.90. Changed resolution and training conditions prevent interpreting the revision as a general same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theorems or proofs. V2's explicit transformer residual equations and reconstruction-loss formula restate operations already depicted or described in v1; notation changes do not establish new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The variable-incremental forecasting contribution remains, but v2 substantially revises its headline efficiency and applicability claims. It replaces approximately 15% trainable parameters with approximately 25%, adds the claim of using half the training data, and introduces claims about real-time adaptation and knowledge distillation. These extend beyond renaming the framework.

C2.justification: V2 adds a temporal-dynamics explanation for loss weighting, contrasting rapidly changing temperature with slower geopotential evolution. It interprets reduced-budget results as supporting operational replacement of conventional training and discusses short-term forecasting weaknesses. V1's interpretation of channel-selection patterns as evidence of expert specialization disappears with Figure 6.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code URL instead of v1's future-release promise and explicitly documents index-embedding expansion and index-encoder retraining. Backbone attribution is revised without clearly specifying an architectural change. AdamW, learning rates, stated epochs, batch size, PyTorch and 16 A100 GPUs remain documented in both.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Aurora, OneForecast, Stormer, probabilistic forecasting and NowcastNet, and replaces some general machine-learning references. The central positioning against fixed-variable weather models and class/task incremental learning remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and substantial method/results passages are rewritten. Task Definition and Method become a unified Methodology section with finer subsections; experiments are reorganized into Main Results, Ablation Study and Visualization. The title, author block and terminology change, and acknowledgements are added.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn, with a new performance panel in Figure 1. Figure 4 changes its legend, axes styling and displayed comparisons. Table 2 adds dataset/iteration columns and pressure-variable results; upper-air comparisons are separated into Tables 3–4. Figure 6 is removed, while Figure 5 is reused with revised placement and caption.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens empirical assessment through comparisons at a common reported resolution and full-training/reduced-data controls, addressing limitations of v1's mixed-resolution comparisons and limited efficiency evidence. Clearer organization and a code URL also help. These gains are tempered by removal of the routing diagnostic and inconsistent efficiency wording: the abstract claims 25% trainable parameters, whereas the contribution list claims 25% fewer parameters.
